L0: # Bonn RGB-D Dynamic Dataset
L1: ### The Bonn RGB-D Dynamic Dataset
L2: Abstract: This is a dataset for RGB-D SLAM, containing highly dynamic sequences. We provide 24 dynamic sequences, where people perform different tasks, such as manipulating boxes or playing with balloons, plus 2 static sequences. For each scene we provide the ground truth pose of the sensor, recorded with an Optitrack Prime 13 motion capture system. The sequences are in the same format as the cite0†TUM RGB-D Dataset†vision.in.tum.de , so that the same evaluation tools can be used.
L3: Furthermore, we provide a ground truth 3D point cloud of the static environment recorded using a Leica BLK360 terrestrial laser scanner.

L20: Ground truth model
L21: We provide the full ground truth point cloud of 394109339 points, as well as a subsampled section of 54676774 points, more convenient for evaluation. The point clouds are in PLY ASCII format. To convert a model from the reference frame of the RGB-D sensor to the one of the ground truth model, refer to the Evaluation section below.

L25: Evaluation
L26: Since the dataset is in the same format as the TUM RGB-D Dataset, for evaluating the trajectory error it is possible to use cite4†the same Python tools†vision.in.tum.de .
L27: 
L28: For evaluating the reconstructed model w.r.t. the ground truth, it is first necessary to transform them to the same coordinate frame. To convert a model from the reference frame of the sensor to the one of the ground truth, one can use the following transformation:
L29: $\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{g}=\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{ROS}^{-1}\mathbf{T}_0\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{ROS}\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{m}$,
L30: where $\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{m}$ is the transformation between the reference frame of the RGB-D sensor and the one of the markers used by the motion capture system, $\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{ROS}$ transforms the coordinate frame of the motion capture system to the one used to write the file groundtruth.txt in the sequences, $\mathbf{T}_0$ is the first pose read from the file groundtruth.txt.
L31: The value of $\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{m}$ obtained from our calibration is the following:
L32: $ \mathbf{T}_\mathrm{m} =
L33: \begin{pmatrix}
L34: 1.0157 & 0.1828 & -0.2389 & 0.0113 \\
L35: 0.0009 & -0.8431 & -0.6413 & -0.0098 \\
L36: -0.3009 & 0.6147 & -0.8085 & 0.0111 \\
L37: 0 & 0 & 0 & 1.0000
L38: \end{pmatrix}
L39: $.
L40: 
L41: $\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{ROS}$ is needed due to a bug in the ROS node that interfaces the framework to the motion capture system, and its value is:
L42: 
L43: $\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{ROS}=
L44: \begin{pmatrix}
L45: -1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
L46: 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
L47: 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
L48: 0 & 0 & 0 & 1
L49: \end{pmatrix}
L50: $.
L51: Finally, $\mathbf{T}_0$ has to be read from the file groundtruth.txt included in the sequence that has to be evaluated.
L52: 
L53: To simplify this process, we provide a cite5†Python script that will compute $\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{g}$ given $\mathbf{T}_0$. The script requires numpy, numpy-quaternion and numba. The three packages can be easily installed with pip.

L0@P0: ReFusion: 3D Reconstruction in Dynamic Environments
L1@P0: for RGB-D Cameras Exploiting Residuals
L2@P0: Emanuele Palazzolo Jens Behley Philipp Lottes Philippe Giguere Cyrill Stachniss `
L3@P0: Abstract— Mapping and localization are essential capabilities
L4@P0: of robotic systems. Although the majority of mapping systems
L5@P0: focus on static environments, the deployment in real-world situations requires them to handle dynamic objects. In this paper,
L6@P0: we propose an approach for an RGB-D sensor that is able to
L7@P0: consistently map scenes containing multiple dynamic elements.
L8@P0: For localization and mapping, we employ an efficient direct
L9@P0: tracking on the truncated signed distance function (TSDF) and
L10@P0: leverage color information encoded in the TSDF to estimate the
L11@P0: pose of the sensor. The TSDF is efficiently represented using
L12@P0: voxel hashing, with most computations parallelized on a GPU.
L13@P0: For detecting dynamics, we exploit the residuals obtained after
L14@P0: an initial registration, together with the explicit modeling of
L15@P0: free space in the model. We evaluate our approach on existing
L16@P0: datasets, and provide a new dataset showing highly dynamic
L17@P0: scenes. These experiments show that our approach often surpass
L18@P0: other state-of-the-art dense SLAM methods. We make available
L19@P0: our dataset with the ground truth for both the trajectory of
L20@P0: the RGB-D sensor obtained by a motion capture system and
L21@P0: the model of the static environment using a high-precision
L22@P0: terrestrial laser scanner. Finally, we release our approach as
L23@P0: open source code.
L24@P0: I. INTRODUCTION
L25@P0: Mapping and localization are essential capabilities of
L26@P0: robotic systems operating in real-world environments. Simultaneous localization and mapping, or SLAM, is usually
L27@P0: solved in an alternating fashion, where one determines the
L28@P0: pose w.r.t. the map built so far and then use the estimated
L29@P0: pose to update the map. SLAM is especially challenging in
L30@P0: dynamic environments, since a robot needs to build a consistent map. This entails estimating simultaneously which parts
L31@P0: of the environment are static or moving. In particular, moving
L32@P0: objects may cause wrong correspondences, deteriorate the
L33@P0: ability to estimate correct poses and hence corrupt the map.
L34@P0: In this paper, we propose ReFusion: a novel approach for
L35@P0: dense indoor mapping that is robust to dynamic elements.
L36@P0: Our approach is completely geometric, and does not rely
L37@P0: on an explicit semantic interpretation of the scene. More
L38@P0: specifically, we do not employ a deep neural network to
L39@P0: detect specific dynamic classes, in contrast to other recent
L40@P0: approaches [14], [1]. In contrast to other recent purely
L41@P0: geometric approaches [13], [15], we do not represent the
L42@P0: model using surfels, but in the form of a truncated sign distance function (TSDF). This allows our technique to directly
L43@P0: generate a mesh of the environment, which can be useful in
L44@P0: Emanuele Palazzolo, Jens Behley, Philipp Lottes and Cyrill Stachniss are
L45@P0: with the University of Bonn, Germany. Philippe Giguere is with the Laval `
L46@P0: University, Quebec, Canada. ´
L47@P0: This work has partly been supported by the DFG under the grant number
L48@P0: FOR 1505: Mapping on Demand, under the grant number BE 5996/1-1, and
L49@P0: under Germany’s Excellence Strategy, EXC-2070 - 390732324 (PhenoRob).

L54@P0: containing dynamics. Center: Reconstructed model without dynamics reprojected onto the two frames from above. Bottom: Final mesh
L55@P0: without the dynamics.
L56@P0: application such as virtual and augmented reality. Moreover,
L57@P0: the TSDF representation can be useful for planning, since it
L58@P0: provides, by definition, the distance to the closest obstacle.
L59@P0: The main contribution of this paper is a novel and efficient
L60@P0: SLAM algorithm, based on a TSDF representation, that is
L61@P0: robust to dynamics via pure geometric filtering. It is inspired
L62@P0: by the work of Canelhas et al. [3] combined with voxel
L63@P0: hashing [11]. We propose to detect dynamics by exploiting
L64@P0: the residuals obtained from the registration, in combination
L65@P0: with the explicit representation of free space in the environment. This allows our approach to be class agnostic, i.e.,
L66@P0: it does not rely on a detector trained on specific categories
L67@P0: of dynamic objects. Moreover, the dynamic objects are not
L68@P0: explicitly tracked, therefore our approach is not limited by
L69@P0: the number of moving objects or by their speed. Fig. 1 shows
L70@P0: two example RGB frames from a dynamic scene and the
L71@P0: resulting model built by our approach.
L72@P0: We evaluated ReFusion on the TUM RGB-D dataset [18],
L73@P0: as well as on our own dataset, showing the versatility and
L74@P0: robustness of our approach, reaching in several scenes equal
L75@P0: or better performance than other dense SLAM approaches.
L76@P0-1: In addition, we publicly release our dataset, containing 24highly-dynamic scenes recorded with an RGB-D sensor,
L77@P1: together with ground truth trajectories obtained using a
L78@P1: motion capture system. Furthermore, we provide a ground
L79@P1: truth 3D model of the static parts of the environment in
L80@P1: the form of a high resolution point cloud acquired with a
L81@P1: terrestrial laser scanner. To the best of our knowledge, this is
L82@P1: the first dataset containing dynamic scenes that also includes
L83@P1: the ground truth model for the static part of the environment.
L84@P1: Finally, we publicly share the open source implementation
L85@P1: of our approach.
L86@P1: In sum, we make two key claims: our RGB-D mapping
L87@P1: approach (i) is robust to dynamic elements in the environment and provides a camera tracking performance on par or
L88@P1: better than state-of-the-art dense SLAM approaches, and (ii)
L89@P1: provides a dense 3D model that contains only the static parts
L90@P1: of the environment, which is more accurate than other stateof-the-art approaches when compared to the ground truth
L91@P1: model.
L92@P1: II. RELATED WORK
L93@P1: With the advent of inexpensive RGB-D cameras, many approaches for mapping using such sensors were proposed [16],
L94@P1: [22]. The seminal paper of Newcombe et al. [10] showed
L95@P1: the prospects of TSDF-based RGB-D mapping by generating
L96@P1: accurate, high detailed maps using only depth information.
L97@P1: It paved the way for several improvements increasing the
L98@P1: versatility and fidelity of RGB-D mapping. As the approach
L99@P1: relies on a fixed voxel grid, volumes that can be mapped
L100@P1: are limited. Subsequent approaches explore compression of
L101@P1: this grid. For instance, Steinbrucker ¨ et al. [17] use an Octree
L102@P1: instead of a voxel grid. Nießner et al. [11], on the other hand,
L103@P1: propose to only allocate voxel blocks close to the mapped
L104@P1: surface, and address them in constant time via hashing.
L105@P1: Kahler ¨ et al. [6] extend the idea of voxel hashing by using
L106@P1: a hierarchy of voxel blocks with different resolutions. To
L107@P1: alleviate the need for raycasting for generating the model
L108@P1: image for registration, Canelhas et al. [3] and Bylow et al. [2]
L109@P1: propose to directly exploit the TSDF for evaluation of the
L110@P1: residuals and computation of the jacobians within the error
L111@P1: minimization.
L112@P1: Besides using a TSDF, another popular representation of
L113@P1: the model are surfels, which are disks with a normal and a
L114@P1: radius. Keller et al. [7] use surfels to represent the model of
L115@P1: the environment. Whelan et al. [21] extend the approach with
L116@P1: a deformation graph, which allows for long-range corrections
L117@P1: of the map via loop closures.
L118@P1: An alternative approach was proposed by Della Corte et
L119@P1: al. [5]. Their approach registers two consecutive RGB-D
L120@P1: frames directly upon each other by minimizing the photometric error. They integrate multiple cues such as depth, color
L121@P1: and normal information in a unified way. Other approaches
L122@P1: exploit image sequences [9], [20].
L123@P1: Usually, mapping approaches assume a static environment
L124@P1: and therefore handle moving objects mostly through outliers
L125@P1: rejection. By discarding information that disagrees with the
L126@P1: current measurements, one can handle implicitly dynamic
L127@P1: objects [10]. Other approaches model the dynamic parts of

L153@P1: estimating the camera pose and whether clusters are static
L154@P1: or dynamic. Bescos et al. [1] combine a geometric approach

L156@P1: dynamics in an ORB-SLAM2 system [8]. Similarly, Runz ¨
L157@P1: et al. [14] exploit deep learning segmentation, refined with
L158@P1: a geometric approach, to detect objects. In addition, they
L159@P1: reconstruct and track detected objects independently.
L160@P1: In contrast to the aforementioned approaches, we propose
L161@P1: a mapping approach robust to dynamics which relies on
L162@P1: the residuals from the registration and on the detected free
L163@P1: space. In this way, our approach is able to detect any kind
L164@P1: of dynamics without relying on specific classes or models,
L165@P1: and without explicitly tracking dynamic objects.
L166@P1: III. OUR APPROACH
L167@P1: Fig. 2 illustrates the key processing steps of the proposed
L168@P1: approach. Given the color and depth information of an RGBD sensor, like Microsoft’s Kinect, we first perform an initial
L169@P1: pose estimation by exploiting directly the TSDF of our
L170@P1: model representation. By observing the residuals obtained
L171@P1: from such registration, we detect the dynamic elements in
L172@P1: the scene. With the filtered sensor information, where we
L173@P1: discard regions containing dynamics, we further refine the
L174@P1: pose of the sensor. With this refined estimated pose, we then
L175@P1: integrate the sensor measurements, i.e., depth and color, into
L176@P1: the model.
L177@P1: A. Model Representation
L178@P1-2: In our approach, we represent the model of the environment using a truncated signed distance function (TSDF) asoriginally proposed by Curless and Levoy [4]. We briefly
L179@P2: recap it here for the sake of a self-contained description. The
L180@P2: idea is to represent the world with a 3D voxel grid in which
L181@P2: each voxel contains a SDF value. The SDF is a function
L182@P2: VSDF(x) : R
L183@P2: 3 → R that returns, given a point in space,
L184@P2: its signed distance to the nearest surface. This distance is
L185@P2: positive if the point is in front of the surface and negative
L186@P2: otherwise. In this way, the surface is implicitly represented
L187@P2: by the set of points for which VSDF(x) = 0. In practice,
L188@P2: the SDF values are truncated to a given maximum value.
L189@P2: In addition to the TSDF, each voxel contains a weight that
L190@P2: represents how reliable the SDF value is at that location,
L191@P2: as well as the color obtained by projecting it onto the
L192@P2: RGB image. The weight allows us to update each voxel
L193@P2: using a running weighted average, leading to an improved
L194@P2: robustness to outliers [4]. The color information enables both
L195@P2: the texturing of the mesh and the use of intensity information
L196@P2: during the registration.
L197@P2: In our implementation, we do not preallocate a 3D voxel
L198@P2: grid of a fixed size. Instead, we allocate voxel dynamically
L199@P2: and index them using a spatial hashing function, similarly
L200@P2: to Nießner et al. [11]. Representing the world sparsely by
L201@P2: only allocating the needed blocks of voxels enables the
L202@P2: reconstruction of larger scenes, while eliminating the need
L203@P2: for restricting the maximum size of the scene in advance.
L204@P2: Note that we process every voxel in parallel on the GPU,
L205@P2: since the voxels are assumed to be mutually independent,
L206@P2: leading to a considerable speed-up of the computations.
L207@P2: B. Pose Estimation
L208@P2: For estimating the pose of the sensor, we use a point-toimplicit approach as proposed independently by Canelhas et
L209@P2: al. [3] and Bylow et al. [2]. In contrast to KinectFusion [10]
L210@P2: and similar methods, our approach does not generate synthetic views from the model. Instead, we use an alternative
L211@P2: technique and directly align an incoming point cloud from
L212@P2: the sensor to the SDF, since the SDF provides by definition
L213@P2: the distance of a point to the closest surface, i.e., it is possible
L214@P2: to directly use the SDF value as an error function. In addition
L215@P2: to the existing point-to-implicit techniques, we exploit the
L216@P2: color information contained in the model to improve the
L217@P2: alignment.
